summary: Discusses problems with multicast in Mobile IPv6, including mobile group listeners and mobile senders using Any-Source and Source-Specific Multicast. It surveys existing approaches. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Multicast sends one copy of a stream to many receivers along a tree of routers. If a receiver moves, or the sender moves, the tree has to be adjusted or the stream stops arriving. This memo describes that problem in detail and reviews the ways people have tried to solve it.

subtitle: The problem of keeping a multicast stream alive when the sender or the receiver moves.

tldr.problem: A multicast stream is delivered along a tree built around the place where the sender and the receivers are, and when either of them moves the tree no longer reaches them.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets out the problem rather than solving it: it separates listener mobility from source mobility, notes that source mobility is the harder case, and reviews the three general approaches and the many proposals built on them.
tldr.outcome: It recommends that future work first solve seamless reception during handovers, then fold multicast into unicast mobility management, and then provide basic source mobility.

today: RFC 5757 is an Informational memo published in February 2010 by the MobOpts Research Group, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a problem statement and a survey of proposals rather than a specification, and it ends with a list of three problems that future work should tackle first.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
Group communication is a building block for a wide range of applications, from content broadcasting and streaming, voice and video conferencing, collaborative environments and massive multiplayer games to the self-organisation of distributed systems and services. Network-layer multicast support is needed whenever globally distributed, scalable, serverless or instantaneous communication is required. The early idea of internet multicasting led to a wide adoption of Deering's host group model, and broadband media delivery is emerging as a typical mass scenario that demands scalability and bandwidth efficiency from multicast routing. Multicast mobility has been a concern for about ten years and has produced many proposals, but there is still no generally accepted solution. Multicast support matters especially in mobile environments, where users share frequency bands of limited capacity, and reception of infotainment streams may soon need wide deployment of mobile multicast services.

Mobility in IPv6 is standardised in the Mobile IPv6 RFCs, which address network-layer changes while moving between wireless domains. Mobile IPv6 only roughly defines multicast mobility, through a remote subscription approach or bidirectional tunnelling via the home agent. Remote subscription suffers from slow handovers, relying on multicast routing to adapt to the handover. Bidirectional tunnelling introduces inefficient overhead and delay through triangular forwarding, because packets are routed through the home agent rather than along shortest paths. Neither has been optimised for large-scale deployment, and a mobile multicast service for a future internet should give close-to-optimal routing at predictable and limited cost, with robustness and a service quality suited to real-time media distribution.

Intricate multicast routing procedures are not easily extensible to satisfy mobility requirements. A client subscribed to a group while making handovers needs the multicast traffic to follow it to its new location, and a mobile source needs the whole delivery tree to comply with or adapt to its changing position. Considerable effort has gone into designs for mobile multicast receivers, while only limited work has been dedicated to multicast source mobility, which poses the more delicate problem.

In multimedia conferences, games and collaborative environments each member commonly acts as both receiver and sender for group communication, and real-time communication places severe temporal requirements on mobility protocols: typical seamless handover scenarios are expected to limit disruption or delay to less than 100 to 150 ms, and jitter disturbance should not exceed 50 ms. A hundred milliseconds is about the duration of a spoken syllable in real-time audio. The document represents the consensus of the MobOpts Research Group and was reviewed by contributors to the IETF MEXT, MBONED and PIM working groups.

The document defines the problem scope for multicast mobility management, and treats single-hop mobility, where a mobile node attaches directly to fixed access routers, as its focus, matching the perspective of Mobile IPv6. Multi-hop mobility, where the node attaches through local access routers and crosses a mobile cloud, inherits the single-hop aspects and adds the complexity of traversing that cloud, which may be handled by encapsulation or flooding; the issues of nested tunnelling or flooding, and of preserving address transparency, need treatment analogous to Mobile IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IPv6 offers two rough answers and neither is good enough. One makes the node re-join the group at its new network, which is slow. The other tunnels all the traffic through the home network, which sends packets the long way round. The memo sets out why neither scales.

sections.title: The General Issues
sections.content:
Multicast communication is divided into Any Source Multicast and Source-Specific Multicast, and the roles of senders and receivers are distinct and asymmetric, since both may individually be mobile. Their interaction is facilitated by a multicast routing protocol such as DVMRP, PIM in sparse mode or with source-specific multicast, bidirectional PIM, or inter-domain prefix advertisements through BGP multiprotocol extensions, while IPv6 clients interact using the multicast listener discovery protocol.

Any solution has to take all of these functional blocks into account. It should enable seamless continuity of multicast sessions when moving from one IPv6 subnet to another, preserve the multicast nature of packet distribution and approximate optimal routing, and support per-flow handover, because the properties and designations of flows can differ, whether because of differing quality-of-service or real-time requirements or because of network conditions that differ for different groups.

Multicast routing adapts dynamically to the topology at the locations of senders and receivers, and current multicast routing protocols may take a time close to seconds to converge after a change of location, depending on the protocol, the router configuration and the shape of the distribution tree. That is far too slow for seamless handovers of interactive or real-time sessions, and any scheme that readjusts routing is bound by that convergence time. It also has to allow for a mobile node moving faster than the protocol state updates.

IP-layer multicast packet distribution is an unreliable service bound to a connectionless transport service, so applications sensitive to loss or jitter need their own countermeasures. Mobile multicast handovers should not add significant packet drops. Because the service is stateless, bi-casting multicast flows does not degrade the transport layer, and applications should implement mechanisms to detect and respond to duplicate datagrams, although individual applications may not be robust against repeated duplicate streams.

Group addresses are generally location transparent, though they may be scoped and some methods embed unicast prefixes or rendezvous point addresses. The addresses of sources are interpreted by the routing infrastructure and by receiver applications, which are often aware of source addresses, so multicast inherits the address duality problem of Mobile IPv6 for source addresses: an address being both a logical node identifier, the home address, and a topological locator, the care-of address. The elements that make up the delivery tree, that is the senders, forwarders and receivers, have to account for this, by using binding caches, extended multicast states or signalling.

Multicast sources operate decoupled from their receivers: a source sends to a group of receivers that are unknown at the network layer, so it operates without a feedback channel. It can neither inquire about the properties of its delivery trees nor learn about the network-layer state of its receivers. In the event of an inter-tree handover a mobile multicast source is therefore vulnerable to losing connectivity to its receivers without noticing. Applying a Mobile IPv6 binding update or return routability procedure would similarly break the semantic of a receiver group remaining unidentified by the source, so it cannot be applied by analogy with unicast.

Despite the complexity of the requirements, multicast mobility management should seek lightweight solutions that are easy to deploy. Deployment of IP multicast has in any case been slow over the past fifteen years even though all major router vendors and operating systems offer implementations, and roll-out is limited in public inter-domain scenarios. A dispute over the layer at which group communication service should reside turned the research community towards application-layer multicast, and that debate overlaps the mobile multicast domain; work by Garyfalos and Almeroth derived from general principles that when mobility is introduced the performance gap between IP-layer and application-layer multicast widens in different metrics by up to a factor of four. Facing deployment complexity, it is desirable that a solution does not change the routing protocols, and that mobility management is handled at edge nodes so that the routing infrastructure stays mobility-agnostic.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things make multicast harder than unicast. The routers have to rebuild the delivery tree, and that takes seconds. And the sender never learns who is receiving, so it cannot tell that it has lost them.

sections.title: Multicast Listener Mobility
sections.content:
A mobile multicast listener entering a new IP subnet needs multicast reception following a handover in real time, which requires transferring the multicast membership context from its old to its new point of attachment. This can be done by re-establishing a tunnel or by transferring the MLD listening state information of the moving interfaces to the new upstream routers. In the latter case three situations arise. In the simplest, packets of some or all of the subscribed groups are already received by other group members in the new network, so the multicast streams flow natively once the node arrives. In the second, the requested multicast service may be supported and enabled in the visited network but the subscribed groups may not be forwarded to it, because they may be scoped or administratively prohibited, so the distribution trees for the desired groups can only be re-joined at a possibly large routing distance. In the third, the new network may not be multicast-enabled at all, or the specific service may be unavailable, so the distribution trees need to be re-joined at a large routing distance by re-establishing a tunnel to a multicast-enabled network node.

The problem of achieving seamless multicast listener handovers is therefore threefold: ensure multicast reception even in visited networks without appropriate multicast support; minimise multicast forwarding delay so that handovers are seamless and fast, since the time available for multicast mobility operations is bound by the handover time left after IPv6 connectivity is regained and in real-time scenarios this may be significantly less than 100 ms; and minimise the packet loss and reordering that result from multicast handover management.

In many wireless regimes it is also desirable to minimise multicast-related signalling, to preserve the limited resources of battery-powered devices and the constrained transmission capacity of the networks, which may lead to a wish to restrict MLD queries towards the node. Multihomed nodes may ensure smooth handovers with a make-before-break approach, which requires a per-interface subscription, facilitated by an MLD join operating on a pre-selected interface. Encapsulation on the path between the upstream router and the receiver may also result in MTU size conflicts, since path MTU discovery is often not supported for multicast and can reduce scalability in networks with many different MTU sizes or introduce denial-of-service exposure, because the originating addresses of ICMPv6 messages cannot be verified for multicast. Without fragmentation at tunnel entry points, this may prevent the group from being forwarded to the destination.

The infrastructure providing multicast services is required to keep traffic following the node without compromising network functionality, so mobility solutions face immediate problems: they must realise native multicast forwarding and, where applicable, conserve network resources and use link-layer multipoint distribution to avoid data redundancy; they must activate link-multipoint services even if the node performs only a layer 2 handover; they must ensure routing convergence even when the node moves rapidly and hands over frequently; and they must avoid avalanche problems and stream multiplication, which can result from replicated tunnel initiation or redundant forwarding at network nodes. Mobility management can also affect multicast routing, for example through erroneous subscriptions following predictive handover operations, slow traffic termination at leaf nodes resulting from MLD query timeouts, or the node departing from a previous network without leaving the subscribed groups. Packet duplication and reordering may follow a change of topology.
sections.plainLanguage: When a listener arrives in a new network, the group traffic has to start flowing there. That means re-joining the group, or tunnelling the traffic in from a network that carries it. It also has to happen quickly, because the handover has already used up much of the time budget.

sections.title: Multicast Source Mobility
sections.content:
A node submitting data to an Any Source Multicast group either forms the root of a source-specific shortest path tree, distributing data towards a rendezvous point or receivers, or forwards data directly down a shared tree, for example through encapsulated PIM register messages or with bidirectional PIM routing. Native forwarding along source-specific delivery trees is bound to the source's topological network address because of reverse path forwarding checks. A mobile multicast source moving to a new subnetwork can only inject data into a previously established delivery tree, which may be a rendezvous-point-based shared tree, or re-initiate construction of a distribution tree for its new location. In the latter case the mobile sender has to proceed without knowing whether the new tree has regained the ability to forward traffic to the group, because of the decoupling of sender and receivers.

A mobile multicast source must therefore provide address transparency at two layers: to comply with reverse path forwarding checks it has to use an address in the source field of the IPv6 basic header that is in topological agreement with the distribution tree being used, and for application transparency the logical node identifier, commonly the home address, must be presented as the packet source address to the transport layer at the receiver. Those requirements, together with the temporal constraints of handovers, pose major problems for route-optimising solutions, and further issues arise from packet loss and from multicast scoping, since a mobile source away from home must respect the scoping restrictions that arise from its home and its visited location.

Intra-domain multicast routing may allow shared trees that reduce mobility-related complexity. A static rendezvous point may allow a mobile source to keep sending data to the group by encapsulating packets to the rendezvous point with its previous topologically correct or home source address, and with bidirectional PIM, intra-domain mobility is transparently provided by bidirectional shared domain-spanning trees, removing the need to tunnel to the rendezvous point. Issues arise in inter-domain multicast whenever notification of source addresses is required between distributed instances of shared trees, because a new care-of address acquired after a handover is necessarily subject to inter-domain record exchange. With an embedded rendezvous point address, as used for inter-domain PIM in sparse mode, a globally appointed primary rendezvous point lets a newly attached mobile source contact it without prior signalling and transmit data in the PIM register tunnel, but multicast route optimisation such as PIM shortcuts then requires protocol operations equivalent to serving a new source.

Source-Specific Multicast has been designed for senders with static source addresses. The source address in a client subscription to a source-specific group is used directly for route identification, so any subscriber is forced to know the topological address of the contributor to the group, and that identification becomes invalid when the topological source address changes under mobility. Client implementations of source filtering must therefore be aware of the mapping of a logical source identifier to its current topological correspondent.

Source mobility for source-specific multicast needs treatment beyond the problem scope of mobile Any Source Multicast. A listener subscribes to a channel identified by a group and a source, and routers build a shortest path tree rooted at that source, so any change of source address requires state updates at all routers on the upstream path and at all receivers in the group. A new tree has to be established that shares paths with the previous one, for example at the receiver side, and because of the decoupling of sender from receivers the client updates needed for switching trees become a severe burden. A source-specific listener may subscribe to or exclude any particular source and wants to rely on the topological correctness of network operations, so any solution should preserve that confidence, which means binding updates for source-specific sources have to prove address correctness in the unicast routing sense, equivalent to binding update security with a correspondent node in Mobile IPv6. The handover distance between successive points of attachment, the step size of the mobile, serves as a measure of complexity, and since source-specific multicast was designed as a lightweight approach, adding mobility management should preserve that leanness by minimising additional signalling overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving a sender is much harder than moving a receiver. The whole tree has to be rebuilt, and every router and receiver on it has to be told. With source-specific multicast, the source's own address is part of the subscription, so a new address is not just a new path but a new subscription everywhere.

sections.title: Existing Approaches and Proposals
sections.content:
Three approaches to mobile multicast are common. Bidirectional tunnelling has the mobile node tunnel all multicast data via its home agent; this fundamental solution hides all movement and results in static multicast trees, and may be employed transparently by listeners and sources, at the cost of triangular routing and possibly significant performance degradation from widely spanned data tunnels. Remote subscription forces the mobile node to re-initiate multicast distribution after a handover, for example by submitting a listener report to the subnet where it attaches; this relies on multicast dynamics to adapt to network changes, but it results in significant service disruption and leads to mobility-driven changes of source addresses, so it cannot support session persistence under multicast source mobility. Agent-based solutions try to balance the two: static agents act as local tunnelling proxies, allowing some inter-agent handover when the node moves, and the outcome is a decelerated inter-tree handover, or tree walking, which needs extra effort to sustain session persistence through address transparency of mobile sources.

Mobile IPv6 introduces bidirectional tunnelling and remote subscription as minimal standard solutions, and various publications suggest using remote subscription for listener mobility while advising bidirectional tunnelling for source mobility, which avoids the tunnel convergence or avalanche problem, where the home agent has to multiply and encapsulate packets for many receivers of the same group even if they are in the same subnetwork. Its drawback is that multicast communication roles are not explicitly known at the network layer and may change unexpectedly. None of these approaches addresses source-specific source mobility, except bidirectional tunnelling.

For listener mobility there are agent-assisted handover proposals for host-based mobility that complement the unicast real-time mobility infrastructure of Fast Mobile IPv6, the M-FMIPv6 work, Hierarchical Mobile IPv6 and context transfer. All of them assume the context state was stored in a network node reachable before and after the move, but there are cases where the node is no longer in contact with the previous network at its new location, such as moving from one walled operator to another, which require a backwards compatible way to recover from loss of connectivity and context based on the node alone. Proxy Mobile IPv6 is multicast transparent in the sense that the node experiences a point-to-point home link fixed at its static local mobility anchor, composed of a unicast tunnel between the anchor and the current mobile access gateway and a point-to-point link from the gateway to the node. A domain of this kind inherits MTU size problems from spanning tunnels at the receiver site, and two avalanche points can be identified: the anchor may have to tunnel data to many gateways, while a gateway may have to forward the same stream to many nodes over individual point-to-point links.

Other approaches cover encapsulation, hybrid architectures and extensions to the listener discovery protocol. Encapsulating multicast data in a unicast point-to-point tunnel lets multicast-agnostic domains be transited, but inherits the tunnel convergence problem and may multiply traffic; multicast-enabled environments can instead use point-to-multipoint encapsulation, with a multicast destination address in the outer header, which avoids the scaling overhead of unicast tunnels, and the tunnel entry point should fragment data packets to avoid MTU size constraints. Hybrid architectures use proxy gateways at the Internet edge as a bridge between mobility-aware native multicast in access networks and mobility-aware group distribution in the core, and the IRTF Scalable Adaptive Multicast research group was developing general architectural approaches for hybrid multicast solutions. On the discovery protocol, the default timer values and robustness variable were not designed for mobility, which gives a slow reaction after a client leave; this may be a disadvantage on wireless links, and some vendors keep a listener node table at the access router that removes the need for query timeouts on leave messages, that is, explicit receiver tracking. A node using predictive handover may send an early done message before the handoff to speed up termination, while router querying lets the state be restored if the prediction was wrong. A listener hold message exchanged between the node and the home agent is proposed to let a proxy or standby membership service stay in the delivery tree while transmission is paused, which some deployed IPTV solutions use with a frame buffer to switch quickly between channels.

For source mobility the proposals fall into three categories. Statically rooted distribution trees follow a shared tree approach, with mobile senders tunnelling their data to mobility-aware rendezvous points; restricted to a single domain this is equivalent to bidirectional tunnelling. Reconstruction of distribution trees builds a completely new tree after the source moves and so has to compensate for the extra tree-building delay, for instance by tunnelling data into a previously established tree until a timer expires. Tree modification schemes extend the root of an existing delivery tree to incorporate the new source location, relying on extra signalling to fix the forwarding states and heal failures in the reverse path forwarding checks. For source-specific multicast, the shared tree approach has been extended by giving the mobility-aware rendezvous points extended routing tables that hold both the home address and the care-of address, so that mobility reintroduces the concept of rendezvous points into source-specific routing. Other proposals reconstruct the shortest path tree on a client notification, distribute session announcements and address changes periodically to clients over an additional control tree rooted at the home agent, and activate source tree handovers on listener requests.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three broad ways to handle it: tunnel everything through the home network, re-join the group at the new location, or put a proxy in the path. Each has a cost, and the proposals in the literature differ mostly in how they combine them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document discusses multicast extensions to mobility and defines no new methods or procedures. Security issues arise from source address binding updates, specifically in the case of source-specific multicast, and threats of hijacking unicast sessions will result from any solution that jointly operates binding updates for unicast and multicast sessions.

Multicast protocols carry a risk of network-based traffic amplification, since an attacker may abuse mobility signalling to inject unwanted traffic into an established multicast distribution infrastructure. These threats are partly mitigated by reverse path forwarding checks in multicast routers, but a multicast or mobility agent that explicitly replicates multicast streams, such as a home agent that multicasts data, may be vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks, so beyond source authentication a rate control on the replicator may be needed to protect the agent and the downstream network.

Mobility protocols also have to consider authentication, authorization and accounting. A node may have been authorized to receive a specific multicast group on one mobile network, and that may not be valid when it attaches to a different network; the node's accounting association may change between attachments, or may be chosen before re-association, and the most appropriate network path may be one that satisfies user preferences such as avoiding a specific network or minimising cost, rather than one that only minimises routing cost, so accounting bindings may need to be considered when performing context transfer. Admission control issues may arise when new care-of source addresses are introduced to source-specific channels: because there is no feedback, the admission and binding updates of mobile multicast sources require autonomously verifiable authentication, which can be achieved for instance with cryptographically generated addresses.

Modifications to protocols, such as to routing, membership, session announcement and control, as well as the introduction of new entities such as multicast mobility agents, can introduce security vulnerabilities and require consideration of issues such as authentication of network entities and methods to mitigate denial of service, in terms of unwanted network traffic, unnecessary consumption of router and host resources, and router and host state and buffers. Future solutions must analyse and address the security implications of supporting mobile multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing a source's address update matters most in source-specific multicast, where a wrong address means the wrong tree. The document also warns that a node which replicates a stream on behalf of others can be used to amplify traffic, so it needs rate limits as well as authentication.

viz.caption: THE THREE PARTS OF SEAMLESS LISTENER HANDOVER

items.title: Keep receiving
items.text: Multicast reception must continue even in visited networks that have no multicast support of their own.

items.title: Be quick
items.text: After IPv6 connectivity is regained the time left for multicast work may be well under 100 ms.

items.title: Lose little
items.text: Packet loss and reordering caused by the handover management must be minimised.
